proposals.name: Answerable curiosity gap
proposals.instruction: Scores high when a specific answer is withheld but the article promises to supply it; low when the central fact is stated plainly. Does not apply when no answerable question is implied.
proposals.rationale: Unresolved, answerable gaps can motivate clicks beyond conventional news-value cues.

proposals.name: Explanatory promise
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline promises causes, mechanisms, context, or “what we know”; low when it reports only an event or result. Does not apply without explanatory framing.
proposals.rationale: Explanatory framing gives readers a reason to open beyond merely learning that an event occurred.

proposals.name: Actionable reader takeaway
proposals.instruction: Scores high when it suggests a concrete action, precaution, choice, or usable advice; low when it offers no reader-directed consequence. Does not apply when no decision or action is implied.
proposals.rationale: Practical takeaways create direct utility, a distinct source of readership motivation.

proposals.name: Direct everyday exposure
proposals.instruction: Scores high when it explicitly connects to ordinary readers’ health, safety, finances, travel, or routines; low when consequences are confined to remote actors or institutions. Does not apply when no everyday consequence is stated.
proposals.rationale: Personal exposure can make otherwise distant events relevant to a broad readership.

proposals.name: Causal chain clarity
proposals.instruction: Scores high when it states or strongly implies a specific cause and consequence; low when it merely lists events or uses vague causation. Does not apply without a causal relationship.
proposals.rationale: Causal clarity helps readers anticipate useful understanding rather than just another event label.

proposals.name: Agency clarity
proposals.instruction: Scores high when an identifiable actor, action, and target are clear; low when the actor or responsibility is obscured. Does not apply to headlines without an agentive event.
proposals.rationale: Clear agency improves comprehension and makes consequences easier to follow.

proposals.name: Claim contestation
proposals.instruction: Scores high when it includes a denial, accusation, competing account, or disputed claim; low when it presents an uncontested assertion. Does not apply when no proposition is capable of dispute.
proposals.rationale: Disputed claims invite verification and engagement without requiring legal proceedings or institutional prominence.

proposals.name: Outcome completeness
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline gives a concrete result or current status; low when it offers only a vague teaser. Does not apply to purely preview-based headlines.
proposals.rationale: Completeness can attract confirmation-seeking readers, while vagueness may suppress interest.

proposals.name: Temporal trajectory
proposals.instruction: Scores high when it depicts explicit change, escalation, reversal, or a next step; low when it describes a static condition. Does not apply without a time-linked development.
proposals.rationale: Change and progression create a story trajectory readers may follow.

proposals.name: Semantic accessibility
proposals.instruction: Scores high when common words and explicit syntax make the proposition immediately understandable; low when jargon, ellipsis, or ambiguity requires decoding. Does not apply without a substantive proposition.
proposals.rationale: Accessible wording reduces decoding cost and can broaden readership.

proposals.name: Contrasting juxtaposition
proposals.instruction: Scores high when two apparently conflicting facts or clauses are placed together; low when the headline advances one uncomplicated direction. Does not apply without an explicit contrast.
proposals.rationale: Contrast creates compact tension not reducible to novelty, crisis, or controversy.

proposals.name: Normative transgression
proposals.instruction: Scores high when conduct is explicitly framed as violating a social or moral norm; low when conduct is neutral or legitimate. Does not apply without identifiable conduct or evaluative framing.
proposals.rationale: Moral evaluation can trigger attention independently of violence, law, or institutional action.

proposals.name: Visualizability
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline names an observable physical scene, object, or action; low when it presents only an abstract proposition. Does not apply without a physical referent.
proposals.rationale: Concrete scenes can generate interest even when conventional news values are weak.

proposals.name: Affected-person voice
proposals.instruction: Scores high when it quotes or foregrounds an affected person’s feelings, testimony, or self-description; low when it uses only institutional or impersonal narration. Does not apply without a person’s perspective.
proposals.rationale: Affected-person testimony can create identification and credibility beyond generic human-interest labeling.

proposals.name: Evidence signal
proposals.instruction: Scores high when it identifies data, a study, image, testimony, or source supporting a claim; low when it offers a bare assertion. Does not apply when the headline makes no evidential claim.
proposals.rationale: Evidence signals can increase trust or curiosity, affecting readership independently of topic prominence.

proposals.name: Slot-order compression
proposals.instruction: <=6-word, context-light headlines suggest lead-slot or container-position treatment.

proposals.name: Telegraphic breaking syntax
proposals.instruction: Omitted articles, auxiliaries, or context mark urgent copy produced under deadline pressure.
proposals.upstream_parent: time of day, staffing, breaking-news workflow

proposals.name: Question-form framing
proposals.instruction: A headline ending in “?” or beginning with “How,” “Why,” or “Could” marks explainer or engagement packaging.

proposals.name: List or service formula
proposals.instruction: Explicit counts, advice verbs, or “what we learned” wording identifies packaged service content.

proposals.name: Continuation/update markers
proposals.instruction: Words such as “next,” “new,” “still,” “after,” or “for now” signal a later position in a running story.

proposals.name: Calendar-event tokens
proposals.instruction: References to elections, holidays, tournaments, or anniversaries reveal coverage tied to a seasonal news cycle.

proposals.name: Official-name density
proposals.instruction: Multiple personal names, titles, governments, or institutions mark copy from a high-priority beat.

proposals.name: Place-first regional framing
proposals.instruction: A headline led by a country, city, or region indicates regional commissioning or time-zone coverage.

proposals.name: Curiosity-oddity vocabulary
proposals.instruction: Words such as “mystery,” “extraordinary,” “beautiful,” or “worries” identify feature or social-promotion packaging.

proposals.name: House-style punctuation
proposals.instruction: Colons, ellipses, quotation marks, or dash constructions used in recurring combinations reveal template or desk conventions.

proposals.name: Curiosity gap
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline establishes clear stakes but withholds a specific answer readers can discover. Scores low when it states the complete outcome; it does not apply when the premise is too vague to identify.
proposals.rationale: Unanswered questions can motivate clicks independently of conventional news value.

proposals.name: Actionable reader utility
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline promises advice, guidance, or information usable in an ordinary reader’s decisions. Scores low when no practical use is implied; it does not apply to purely descriptive stories.
proposals.rationale: Practical usefulness can drive readership even without crisis, celebrity, or institutional importance.

proposals.name: Direct self-relevance
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when readers can reasonably see effects on their own safety, money, rights, or routines. Scores low when relevance is remote; it does not apply when reader impact cannot be inferred.
proposals.rationale: Personal consequences may predict clicks better than geographic or institutional importance.

proposals.name: Identity resonance
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline invokes a recognizable group identity or shared social experience. Scores low when no audience group is implicated; it does not apply when identity is incidental.
proposals.rationale: Group-based relevance can attract readers without relying on domestic relevance or elite actors.

proposals.name: Emotional intensity
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when wording directly evokes strong fear, empathy, anger, joy, disgust, or awe. Scores low when emotionally neutral; it does not apply when emotion requires information absent from the headline.
proposals.rationale: Emotional arousal can increase readership independently of violence or crisis.

proposals.name: Social conversation potential
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline presents a claim, dispute, or behavior likely to invite opinions or sharing. Scores low for self-contained facts; it does not apply without an evident social reaction.
proposals.rationale: Conversation value may make stories popular despite modest conventional news significance.

proposals.name: Unresolved narrative tension
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when an unfolding situation has a consequential next step or uncertain resolution. Scores low when the event is closed; it does not apply to static explainers.
proposals.rationale: Suspense can sustain reader interest beyond recency or running-story status.

proposals.name: Referent familiarity
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when named people, places, organizations, or objects are broadly recognizable from the headline alone. Scores low when all referents are obscure; it does not apply when familiarity cannot be judged.
proposals.rationale: Recognizable anchors reduce the effort required to decide to click.

proposals.name: Immediate comprehensibility
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when a general reader can understand the basic event on first reading. Scores low when syntax or terminology obscures it; it does not apply when specialist knowledge is explicitly expected.
proposals.rationale: Easily parsed headlines lower the cognitive cost of readership.

proposals.name: Context independence
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline remains meaningful without knowing earlier coverage or surrounding page context. Scores low when references are unexplained; it does not apply to headlines whose context is fully supplied.
proposals.rationale: Standalone meaning can determine whether readers click from a homepage.

proposals.name: Concrete consequence
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline names a tangible outcome readers can imagine or evaluate. Scores low when consequences remain abstract; it does not apply when no outcome is claimed.
proposals.rationale: Concrete stakes make importance legible without depending on institutional action.

proposals.name: Visualizability
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the wording evokes a specific scene, object, or observable action. Scores low when it describes only abstractions; it does not apply when no visual depiction is suggested.
proposals.rationale: Easily imagined scenes may attract attention independently of topic importance.

proposals.name: Explicit audience address
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline directly addresses readers or frames the issue through their possible choices or questions. Scores low when no audience engagement is invited; it does not apply to impersonal statements.
proposals.rationale: Direct address can create click motivation without conventional editorial news values.

proposals.name: Normative judgment invitation
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when readers are prompted to assess fairness, responsibility, harm, or appropriateness. Scores low when the wording is normatively neutral; it does not apply when judgment depends on missing context.
proposals.rationale: Moral evaluation can generate readership even when the event lacks scale or recency.

proposals.name: Interpersonal conflict
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high when two or more identifiable people or groups are clearly positioned against one another. Scores low for solitary or impersonal events; it does not apply when opposition is only implied.
proposals.rationale: Clear human opposition can create engagement beyond formal controversy or institutional action.

proposals.name: Headline brevity
proposals.instruction: Count the headline’s words; classify it as unusually short or unusually long relative to the set.

proposals.name: Question-mark ending
proposals.instruction: Mark whether the headline ends with a question mark.

proposals.name: Colon-led topic prefix
proposals.instruction: Mark whether the headline begins with a topic or series label followed by a colon.

proposals.name: Quotation-mark formatting
proposals.instruction: Mark whether the headline contains quoted speech or a quoted phrase.

proposals.name: Explainer-template opener
proposals.instruction: Mark headlines beginning with templates such as “Why”, “How”, “What we know”, or “Six reasons”.

proposals.name: Continuation cue
proposals.instruction: Mark explicit update or sequel wording such as “new”, “next”, “after”, “despite”, or “again”.

proposals.name: Calendar-event marker
proposals.instruction: Mark explicit references to a named sporting, cultural, or seasonal event.

proposals.name: Geographic marker
proposals.instruction: Mark whether the headline names a country, city, region, or demonym.

proposals.name: Celebrity-name marker
proposals.instruction: Mark whether the headline names a celebrity, entertainer, or entertainment programme.

proposals.name: Crisis-boilerplate wording
proposals.instruction: Mark explicit crisis terms such as “kills”, “dead”, “attack”, “arrested”, “fire”, or “missing”.

proposals.name: Curiosity Gap
proposals.instruction: High when the headline withholds a central cause, outcome, or explanation; low when it fully resolves the story. Does not apply without an identifiable information gap.
proposals.rationale: Unresolved information can motivate readers to click for closure.

proposals.name: Explanatory Promise
proposals.instruction: High when the headline promises reasons, context, consequences, or what happens next; low when it merely announces an event. Does not apply without an implied explanation.
proposals.rationale: Readers may select stories that answer an explicit or implicit question.

proposals.name: Practical Utility
proposals.instruction: High when the headline offers information usable for decisions or actions; low when it has no practical application. Does not apply when no advice or actionable implication appears.
proposals.rationale: Utility can drive readership independently of conventional news importance.

proposals.name: Immediate Personal Stakes
proposals.instruction: High when ordinary readers’ safety, health, rights, finances, or routines are directly affected; low when consequences are remote. Does not apply without a plausible everyday consequence.
proposals.rationale: Direct personal consequences are stronger click incentives than abstract public significance.

proposals.name: Emotional Language
proposals.instruction: High when wording explicitly conveys fear, anger, grief, joy, disgust, or hope; low when emotionally neutral. Does not apply when no affective language is present.
proposals.rationale: Explicit emotion may predict attention beyond the underlying event category.

proposals.name: Moral Polarization
proposals.instruction: High when the headline clearly frames blame, injustice, hypocrisy, or a right-versus-wrong dispute; low when it remains evaluatively neutral. Does not apply without moral evaluation.
proposals.rationale: Moral judgment can attract readers even without crisis, violence, or elite actors.

proposals.name: Identity Resonance
proposals.instruction: High when readers can readily see themselves as members of the affected group; low when no recognizable group identity is invoked. Does not apply without an explicit or strongly implied group.
proposals.rationale: Self-relevant identity cues can increase readership beyond geographic relevance.

proposals.name: Interpersonal Conflict
proposals.instruction: High when identifiable people accuse, betray, oppose, or emotionally confront one another; low when events are impersonal. Does not apply without a person-to-person dispute.
proposals.rationale: Relational drama supplies narrative tension not captured by institutional action alone.

proposals.name: First-Person Voice
proposals.instruction: High when a participant’s quoted words or personal perspective is central; low when the headline uses detached narration. Does not apply without direct personal voice.
proposals.rationale: Personal testimony can create immediacy, intimacy, and curiosity.

proposals.name: Humor or Playfulness
proposals.instruction: High when wording uses humor, irony, wordplay, or an amusing premise; low when strictly literal and formal. Does not apply when neither humor nor playfulness is evident.
proposals.rationale: Entertainment value can make low-importance stories highly clickable.

proposals.name: Taboo or Shock
proposals.instruction: High when the subject explicitly violates sexual, bodily, social, or cultural norms; low when conventionally acceptable. Does not apply without a salient norm violation.
proposals.rationale: Transgressive content can attract attention independently of standard news values.

proposals.name: Shareability Cue
proposals.instruction: High when the headline signals a meme, viral moment, striking image, online trend, or participatory phenomenon; low for ordinary reporting. Does not apply without an explicit social-diffusion cue.
proposals.rationale: Perceived shareability can increase readership through curiosity and social attention.

proposals.name: Visual Vividness
proposals.instruction: High when the headline evokes a concrete, unusual, or easily imagined scene; low when it is abstract or bureaucratic. Does not apply when imagery cannot be inferred from the wording.
proposals.rationale: Vivid mental imagery can make a headline more attention-grabbing.

proposals.name: Protagonist Agency
proposals.instruction: High when a clearly identified person deliberately performs a consequential action; low when the headline describes passive events or systems. Does not apply without an identifiable human agent.
proposals.rationale: Agent-centered narratives are easier to follow and may invite readers into a story.

proposals.name: Processing Fluency
proposals.instruction: High when the headline is immediately clear, grammatical, and concrete; low when ambiguous, fragmented, or syntactically difficult. Does not apply when clarity cannot be judged from the headline alone.
proposals.rationale: Easily processed headlines may receive more clicks under limited reader attention.

proposals.name: Telegraphic compression
proposals.instruction: Omits articles, auxiliaries, or grammatical subjects, producing a clipped fragment.

proposals.name: Question-form framing
proposals.instruction: Uses a direct question rather than a declarative headline.

proposals.name: List/explainer scaffolding
proposals.instruction: Uses forms such as “why,” “how,” “what we know,” or a numbered list.

proposals.name: Colon package label
proposals.instruction: Begins with a named package, event, or topic followed by a colon.

proposals.name: Acronym-heavy shorthand
proposals.instruction: Contains multiple unexplained initials or compressed forms such as PM, MPs, or N Korea.
proposals.upstream_parent: copy-desk space constraints or house style

proposals.name: Quoted personal voice
proposals.instruction: Includes a first-person statement or a short quotation attributed to a person.

proposals.name: Distant-place density
proposals.instruction: Names a foreign country, city, or region without a direct UK location cue.

proposals.name: Immediate-event connector
proposals.instruction: Uses temporal links such as “after,” “amid,” “following,” or “new” to signal a recent development.

proposals.name: Running-story continuation cue
proposals.instruction: Frames the item as a follow-up, update, consequence, or unresolved next step, using wording such as “what happens next” or “what we learned.”
proposals.upstream_parent: position/order within a multi-day running story

proposals.name: Calendar-event branding
proposals.instruction: Names a recurring scheduled event or seasonal occasion as the headline’s organizing label.
proposals.upstream_parent: seasonal news cycle or event desk

proposals.name: Unanswered question
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline withholds a specific answer readers can seek by clicking; low when it states the answer or presents no clear information gap. It does not apply when no answerable issue is implied.
proposals.rationale: Curiosity gaps can increase readership independently of novelty, crisis, or editorial prominence.

proposals.name: Practical utility
proposals.instruction: Scores high when reading promises guidance for an action, decision, or immediate problem; low when it offers only description or reaction. It does not apply when no reader action or decision is implicated.
proposals.rationale: Useful information can attract readers even without dramatic events or prominent actors.

proposals.name: Explanatory promise
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline promises reasons, mechanisms, or consequences behind a clearly named phenomenon; low when it merely announces an event or status. It does not apply when no explanation is implied.
proposals.rationale: Explanatory value may motivate clicks beyond the listed news-value criteria.

proposals.name: Direct personal consequence
proposals.instruction: Scores high when ordinary readers can infer a concrete effect on their safety, rights, relationships, or daily choices; low when consequences remain remote or unspecified. It does not apply when no reader-facing consequence is suggested.
proposals.rationale: Perceived self-relevance is a direct pathway to readership.

proposals.name: Context independence
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline supplies enough referents and relationships to understand the story without prior coverage; low when it relies on unexplained shorthand or assumed background. It does not apply when missing context cannot be judged from the wording.
proposals.rationale: Readers are more likely to click headlines they can immediately interpret.

proposals.name: Semantic clarity
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the subject, action, and main implication are unambiguous on first reading; low when syntax or meaning permits competing interpretations. It does not apply when the headline is too fragmentary to assess.
proposals.rationale: Clear meaning reduces friction between seeing a headline and choosing to read.

proposals.name: Cognitive ease
proposals.instruction: Scores high when common words and familiar syntax permit rapid processing; low when jargon, dense modifiers, or convoluted construction dominate. It does not apply when difficulty comes solely from an unavoidable proper name.
proposals.rationale: Processing fluency can affect clicks separately from story importance.

proposals.name: Emotional arousal
proposals.instruction: Scores high when wording evokes strong fear, anger, grief, hope, disgust, or joy; low when it is emotionally neutral. It does not apply when emotional tone is indeterminate.
proposals.rationale: Emotional activation can increase attention without requiring crisis or violence.

proposals.name: Moral judgment cue
proposals.instruction: Scores high when wording invites judgment about wrongdoing, unfairness, hypocrisy, or victimization; low when it reports without normative implication. It does not apply when no evaluative or blame cue appears.
proposals.rationale: Moral evaluation can create readership motivation beyond legal or institutional content.

proposals.name: Narrative tension
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline presents a clear conflict, reversal, dilemma, or unresolved predicament; low when it describes a straightforward stable state. It does not apply when no relational tension is present.
proposals.rationale: Tension encourages readers to seek development or resolution.

proposals.name: Visual imaginability
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the words evoke a specific scene, object, or action readily pictured; low when abstract states or concepts dominate. It does not apply when no concrete referent is supplied.
proposals.rationale: Vivid mental imagery can make otherwise ordinary headlines more attention-getting.

proposals.name: Identity resonance
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline explicitly invokes group membership, values, or identity concerns; low when no identity cue is present. It does not apply when relevant identities cannot be inferred from the headline.
proposals.rationale: Identity relevance can motivate readership beyond geographic domestic relevance.

proposals.name: Conversational potential
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline contains a contestable claim, dispute, or stance likely to prompt discussion; low when it offers no evident conversational hook. It does not apply when no position or disagreement is expressed.
proposals.rationale: Discussion value can drive readership even when conventional news values are weak.

proposals.name: First-person testimony
proposals.instruction: Scores high when a personal account or direct individual voice is foregrounded; low when narration is entirely impersonal or institutional. It does not apply when no attributable personal voice appears.
proposals.rationale: Perceived firsthand access can increase interest independently of human-interest subject matter.

proposals.name: Attribution transparency
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline clearly identifies who makes a claim and whether it is alleged, disputed, or confirmed; low when contentious claims lack attribution or qualification. It does not apply to straightforward uncontested reports.
proposals.rationale: Trust-relevant framing may influence whether readers choose to investigate a headline.

proposals.name: Headline length
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Count the words in the headline, excluding punctuation.

proposals.name: Question-form framing
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Mark yes if the headline is grammatically phrased as a question or ends with a question mark.

proposals.name: Explainer or listicle cue
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Mark yes if it uses explicit explanatory or list framing such as “why,” “how,” “what we know,” or a numbered reason structure.

proposals.name: Direct-quote framing
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Mark yes if quotation marks contain a speaker’s words, testimony, or evaluative phrase.

proposals.name: House-style punctuation
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Record whether the headline uses a colon, em dash, ellipsis, or other distinctive punctuation pattern.

proposals.name: Named-entity lead
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Mark yes if the headline begins with a named person, organisation, country, city, or other proper noun.

proposals.name: Entertainment-beat marker
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Mark yes if it explicitly signals celebrities, film, music, television, games, or other entertainment coverage.

proposals.name: Numerical-detail format
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Mark yes if the headline prominently contains an age, casualty count, date, monetary amount, percentage, or other numeral.

proposals.name: Geographic-desk marker
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Mark yes if a country, city, nationality, or regional label is a prominent headline element.

proposals.name: Continuity or sequence cue
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Mark yes if it contains wording such as “again,” “what happens next,” “what we know,” “latest,” or “for now,” suggesting a running story or slot sequence.
proposals.upstream_parent: multi-day story position or day-run placement

proposals.name: Overt clickbait curiosity hook
proposals.instruction: Headlines ending in an ellipsis or posing a direct question to the reader score high; straightforward factual statements score low. Does not apply to rhetorical quotes.
proposals.rationale: Explicit curiosity gaps directly incentivize reader clicks, strongly predicting same-outlet readership.

proposals.name: Direct address to the reader
proposals.instruction: Headlines using second-person pronouns (you, your) or direct imperatives score high. Institutional or third-person reports score low.
proposals.rationale: Direct address personalizes the news, increasing perceived relevance and likelihood of a reader clicking.

proposals.name: High-imagination novelty
proposals.instruction: Scores high for unusual, surprising, or bizarre objects/animals (e.g., mosquitoes, dragons). Scores low for standard political or institutional topics.
proposals.rationale: Readers frequently click on highly unusual, "lighter" novelty stories to break from heavy news cycles.

proposals.name: UK domestic consumer impact
proposals.instruction: Scores high if detailing immediate disruptions to UK daily life (money, weather, infrastructure). Otherwise scores low.
proposals.rationale: BBC readers heavily click stories detailing immediate disruptions to their daily routines and local environments.

proposals.name: Stranger-than-fiction human true crime
proposals.instruction: Scores high for bizarre individual acts or survival stories. Scores low for mass casualty or institutional crime.
proposals.rationale: Audiences are drawn to intimate, dramatic individual narratives over broad, ambiguous institutional violence.

proposals.name: Technological or digital scandal
proposals.instruction: Scores high for stories about hacks, apps, or digital culture. Scores low for traditional infrastructure or politics.
proposals.rationale: Tech stories often blend novelty with personal digital risk, driving high click-through rates.

proposals.name: Subjective extremity or superlatives
proposals.instruction: Headlines using absolute adjectives (longest, most, world's) score high; neutral, factual reporting scores low. Does not apply to numbers.
proposals.rationale: Superlatives promise an extreme or record-breaking experience, effectively teasing a must-read story.

proposals.name: Viral quote or social media hook
proposals.instruction: Scores high if the core news is a controversial or viral statement (often in quotes). Scores low for physical events.
proposals.rationale: Readers click to see the context of highly emotional or controversial viral statements.

proposals.name: Absent subject or teaser ellipsis
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the main subject is hidden ("...for now"). Scores low when subjects are explicitly named.
proposals.rationale: Hiding the story's payoff creates an open curiosity gap that directly motivates the reader to click.

proposals.name: Geopolitical threat to the West
proposals.instruction: Scores high for direct, unprecedented military threats to North America or Europe. Scores low for distant regional conflicts.
proposals.rationale: Audiences click heavily on international news when it implies a direct, escalating threat to their security.

proposals.name: UK political rebellion or scandal
proposals.instruction: Scores high for UK politicians breaking ranks or personal scandals. Scores low for routine diplomatic or policy news.
proposals.rationale: BBC readers display a strong appetite for domestic political drama and internal government conflict.

proposals.name: Superstar celebrity name recognition
proposals.instruction: Scores high only for global A-list celebrities. Scores low for niche public figures, politicians, or minor journalists.
proposals.rationale: Famous names act as immediate heuristic triggers for readers seeking entertainment or soft news.

proposals.name: Absence of named foreign locations
proposals.instruction: Scores high for vague, relatable zones (deep space, remote islands). Scores low for specific foreign cities. Does not apply to UK/US locations.
proposals.rationale: Readers often bypass heavily foreign geographic news unless tied to a universal human hook.

proposals.name: Negativity bias in violence
proposals.instruction: Scores high for intentional murder or beheading. Scores low for accidental mass deaths like fires or stampedes.
proposals.rationale: Readers are psychologically drawn to intentional, dramatic violence over tragic but accidental large-scale events.

proposals.name: Implicit domestic relevance comparison
proposals.instruction: Scores high when comparing a foreign event directly to the UK or US. Scores low for isolated foreign events.
proposals.rationale: Framing foreign events as relevant to the reader's home country drastically increases their likelihood of clicking.

proposals.name: Routine foreign disaster reports
proposals.instruction: Headline describes a mass-casualty event (factory fire, stampede) located outside the UK without named individuals.

proposals.name: Elites in diplomatic disputes
proposals.instruction: Focuses on government officials (PM, President) in routine negotiations, abstract agreements, or blame-shifting.

proposals.name: Hard-news titles on soft stories
proposals.instruction: Presents a service, explainer, or pop-culture piece using a provocative, urgent, or curiosity-gap question format.

proposals.name: Named crime or crisis victims
proposals.instruction: Headline specifies the victim's age, gender, or relationship (e.g., "girl of two", "husband") rather than an anonymous casualty count.

proposals.name: UK domestic social policy
proposals.instruction: Focuses on local infrastructure, legal rulings, or safety issues specifically naming UK regions or funds.

proposals.name: Bizarre tech or internet novelty
proposals.instruction: Headline features an unusual, specific digital event, app, or internet meme presented as a standalone oddity.

proposals.name: Retrospective biography hooks
proposals.instruction: Focuses on a historical or completed event framed as an explainer, anniversary, or personal retrospective.

proposals.name: Viral reactions or analogies
proposals.instruction: Headline uses quotation marks to highlight an outraged reaction, or makes an explicit film/pop-culture comparison.

proposals.name: Institutional impact of individual acts
proposals.instruction: Isolated attacks, accidents, or crimes are framed primarily by the resulting corporate or government policy response.

proposals.name: Quoted emotional micro-narrative
proposals.instruction: Headline features a direct quote expressing helplessness, outrage, or despair without naming the broader institutional context.

proposals.name: First-person direct quote
proposals.instruction: Scores high if the headline opens with a direct quote containing first-person pronouns; scores low for purely descriptive headlines. Does not apply if quotes are third-person institutional statements.
proposals.rationale: Direct vulnerability and personal testimony drive high reader empathy and click-through rates.

proposals.name: Superlative and absolute framing
proposals.instruction: Scores high for phrases like "world's longest", "most beautiful", or "all US". Scores low if magnitude is qualified or absent.
proposals.rationale: Extreme claims trigger high curiosity and urgency, prompting immediate reader engagement and clicks.

proposals.name: Curiosity gap via unresolved question
proposals.instruction: Scores high if headline ends in a question mark or implies a hidden explanation (e.g., "mystery of"). Scores low for straightforward factual summaries.
proposals.rationale: Information gaps compel users to click to resolve the cognitive uncertainty created by the headline.

proposals.name: Absurdity or bizarre juxtaposition
proposals.instruction: Scores high for unexpected combinations of mundane and extreme concepts (e.g., lotto and therapy, planes and homesickness). Scores low for typical news narratives.
proposals.rationale: High novelty, weirdness, or irony serves as strong clickbait for casual readers seeking entertainment.

proposals.name: Exploitation of digital or cyber fear
proposals.instruction: Scores high if the text highlights digital vulnerabilities, hacking, or malicious apps affecting personal safety. Scores low for physical or corporate threats.
proposals.rationale: Personal cyber threats trigger visceral, broadly relatable fears that drive high individual readership.

proposals.name: Domestic everyday life impact
proposals.instruction: Scores high if focusing on routine consumer realities (e.g., food brands, local restrictions, housing). Scores low for distant geopolitical events lacking personal stakes.
proposals.rationale: Readers click heavily on news directly affecting their daily environment, routines, and purchasing habits.

proposals.name: Pop culture and reality drama
proposals.instruction: Scores high for names of celebrities, TV shows, or entertainment gossip. Scores low for serious political or institutional updates.
proposals.rationale: Soft news and celebrity drama provide a highly clickable escape from hard political or economic news.

proposals.name: Child as central victim or hero
proposals.instruction: Scores high if the headline explicitly features a child as a victim or primary actor. Scores low if casualties are anonymous or adult-only.
proposals.rationale: Crimes or tragedies involving children provoke exceptionally strong emotional reactions and reader clicks.

proposals.name: Unusual mode of mass death
proposals.instruction: Scores high for mass casualties caused by novel, bizarre events (e.g., zoo fires, stampedes). Scores low for standard warfare, generic shootings, or accidents.
proposals.rationale: Novelty in tragedy leverages morbid curiosity, driving more clicks than routine disaster reports.

proposals.name: Explainer or analytical framing
proposals.instruction: Scores high for phrases like "what happens next", "what we learned", or "six reasons". Scores low for breaking or developing factual updates.
proposals.rationale: Analytical context and listicles attract readers seeking deep understanding or easily digestible summaries.

proposals.name: Explicit named geographic conflict zone
proposals.instruction: Scores high if headline names a specific foreign country in active conflict (e.g., Ukraine). Scores low for domestic or non-conflict foreign news.
proposals.rationale: High-profile international conflicts represent ongoing major stories that consistently attract intense reader attention.

proposals.name: Outrage-inducing social betrayal
proposals.instruction: Scores high for powerful figures persecuting whistleblowers, or gross injustice. Scores low for standard legal proceedings or balanced political debate.
proposals.rationale: Stories highlighting institutional betrayal or unfairness strongly motivate readers to click and share.

proposals.name: Featured human survival narrative
proposals.instruction: Scores high if text highlights an individual surviving or escaping a life-threatening event. Scores low for purely statistical reports of death or destruction.
proposals.rationale: Reader click-behavior strongly favors individual survival and human interest over abstract casualty statistics.

proposals.name: Prominent trusted celebrity figure
proposals.instruction: Scores high if a globally recognized entertainment figure is the explicit subject. Scores low for generic celebrities or politicians.
proposals.rationale: Readers have high parasocial investment in specific mega-stars, driving clicks independent of the topic.

proposals.name: Vague but severe institutional charge
proposals.instruction: Scores high for generic but alarming institutional accusations (e.g., "fake", "treated like slaves"). Scores low if accusations are legalistic or procedurally vague.
proposals.rationale: Broad, emotionally resonant accusations generate immediate reader outrage more effectively than complex policies.

proposals.name: NAMED-ENTITY VAGUENESS
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Headline names no specific person, country, or institution, relying instead on broad placeholders (e.g., "this place", "celebs", "stars") or abstract references.

proposals.name: INVERSION OF TRAGEDY STRUCTURE
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: A grave action (death, violence, disaster) appears in a dependent clause at the end, preceded by an institutional subject or summary rather than opening the text.
proposals.upstream_parent: Daily run position or late-cycle wrap-up

proposals.name: NEGATIVE-CONSEQUENCE CLOSER
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Headline begins with a soft, novelty, or celebrity element, but ends with a tragic, fatal, or violent noun (e.g., "after murder", "after attacks").
proposals.upstream_parent: Editorial placement or multi-day story evolution

proposals.name: OMITTED GEOGRAPHIC ANCHOR
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Headline describes a mass-casualty event, crime, or crisis without naming the country or city where it occurred (e.g., using only "factory", "zoo").
proposals.upstream_parent: Foreign desk beat relying on homepage promotion

proposals.name: ABSTRACT INSTITUTIONAL ACTION
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Headline describes high-level political or bureaucratic processes using verbs like "votes", "accuses", "unveils", or "quits" without naming affected victims or concrete consequences.

proposals.name: LIGHT-HEADED INTERROGATIVE FORMAT
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Headline is phrased as a direct question ("Will this...?", "Why do...?") combined with soft, historical, or scientific subject matter rather than immediate crises.

proposals.name: REGIONAL POLICY SHORTHAND
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Headline uses metonymy or specific geographic shorthand (e.g., "swathes of northern England", "US within missile range") to summarize domestic impact.

proposals.name: SUPERLATIVE-LED NOVELTY
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Headline opens with or heavily features a superlative ("most beautiful", "longest", "strictest") for a story that is otherwise low-stakes or historical.

proposals.name: QUOTATION-LED EMOTIONALITY
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: The headline begins directly with a quote expressing helplessness, outrage, or shock, followed by an em-dash identifying the speaker.

proposals.name: NARRATIVE OR CHARACTER EPIPHET
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Headline frames the subject using descriptive titles, age, or narrative tropes (e.g., "homesick mechanic", "9-year-old", "Selfie Kid") rather than institutional roles.

proposals.name: Narrative curiosity gap
proposals.instruction: Headlines scoring high use partial reveals or explicit interrogatives ("How", "Why", "What we learned"). Does not apply to straightforward, declarative event reporting.
proposals.rationale: Readers click to satisfy specific curiosity triggered by unresolved, hinted narratives.

proposals.name: Personal vulnerability
proposals.instruction: Scores high if focusing on a specific child, family, or isolated victim facing severe distress. Low for abstract institutional updates or statistics.
proposals.rationale: Emotional empathy for identifiable, highly vulnerable individuals drives robust readership and clicks.

proposals.name: Juxtaposed absurdity
proposals.instruction: High scores feature bizarre or ironic contrasts (e.g., gadget hack, homesick mechanic). Does not apply to expected geopolitical or domestic news events.
proposals.rationale: Novelty and incongruity act as strong cognitive magnets for casual readers seeking surprise.

proposals.name: Pop-culture celebrity novelty
proposals.instruction: Scores high for A-list celebrities interacting with non-news domains (e.g., sports, interviews). Low for routine celebrity sightings or deaths.
proposals.rationale: Audience parasocial interest spikes when famous figures do unexpected or relatable things.

proposals.name: Anthropomorphised animals
proposals.instruction: Scores high if animals act bizarrely or show human-like agency. Does not apply to standard wildlife or ecological reporting.
proposals.rationale: Readers inherently click on novel animal stories for entertainment, seeking emotional relief.

proposals.name: Unique superlatives
proposals.instruction: High if claiming an absolute "first", "longest", or "most" regarding a feat. Low for generic events without an extreme frame.
proposals.rationale: Extremes naturally attract human attention by breaking established boundaries and promising unique content.

proposals.name: Strong emotive quotation
proposals.instruction: Scores high if featuring first-person quotes expressing helplessness or extreme anger. Low for neutral, institutional statements or policy quotes.
proposals.rationale: Raw human emotion in quotes creates immediate psychological impact, encouraging deeper story engagement.

proposals.name: Foreboding future tense
proposals.instruction: High if predicting catastrophic future scenarios or escalating conflicts. Low for immediate, resolved past events or routine updates.
proposals.rationale: Impending crises trigger anticipatory anxiety, compelling readers to seek immediate threat information.

proposals.name: UK domestic consumer impact
proposals.instruction: Scores high for local restrictions or costs directly affecting UK wallets. Low for foreign policies with no immediate local consumer consequence.
proposals.rationale: Readers prioritize practical news that alters their daily routines or personal financial security.

proposals.name: Geopolitical hard-news ambiguity
proposals.instruction: High for breaking elite state actions or explicit major threats. Low for soft news, features, or expected diplomatic friction.
proposals.rationale: Readers rapidly click unambiguous, major geopolitical shifts to understand immediate global stability.

proposals.name: Acute technological anxiety
proposals.instruction: High for tech threats evoking danger (hacks, surveillance, deepfakes). Low for tech business updates or benign scientific discoveries.
proposals.rationale: Digital threats feel highly personal and immediate, triggering strong threat-assessment impulses.

proposals.name: Relatable utilitarian advice
proposals.instruction: Scores high for actionable advice on unexpected life events or mental health. Low for abstract concepts lacking personal utility.
proposals.rationale: Audiences click to acquire practical survival strategies, wealth preservation, or psychological tips.

proposals.name: Bureaucratic political process
proposals.instruction: Scores low if describing routine administrative politics without explicit, character-driven conflict. Does not apply to policy changes.
proposals.rationale: Readers often ignore procedural, ideological, or administrative updates lacking immediate stakes.

proposals.name: Institutional hypocrisy accusation
proposals.instruction: Scores high if explicitly accusing leaders or states of hypocrisy or fake charges. Low for standard policy disagreements or neutral facts.
proposals.rationale: Moral outrage directed at perceived elite hypocrisy is a highly viral, click-driving emotion.

proposals.name: Opaque entity ambiguity
proposals.instruction: Scores low if vague pronouns obscure the main subject unless part of a curiosity gap. Does not apply if the topic is known.
proposals.rationale: Unresolved topical ambiguity frustrates readers who prefer headlines delivering immediate context.

proposals.name: Direct quote attribution
proposals.instruction: Headline contains quotation marks around a segment of speech, likely indicating an exclusive interview or editorialized comment.

proposals.name: Institutional process verbs
proposals.instruction: Headline relies on procedural political verbs like quits, votes out, or congratulates, lacking immediate crisis.

proposals.name: Geographic ambiguity of crisis
proposals.instruction: Headline mentions death or violence in a location distant from the UK without naming elite actors.

proposals.name: Domestic policy domain cues
proposals.instruction: Headline references local geographic scopes like swathes of northern England without naming specific elite individuals.

proposals.name: Superlative listicle framing
proposals.instruction: Headline poses a question or promises a list using extreme adjectives like most or longest.

proposals.name: Abstract novelty entities
proposals.instruction: Headline focuses on quirky animals, space anomalies, or bizarre tech hacks without institutional or human consequences.

proposals.name: High-recency breaking markers
proposals.instruction: Headline uses vague terminology for ongoing events like operation, spread, or attack without finalized outcomes.
proposals.upstream_parent: Story position in a daily cycle

proposals.name: Abbreviated agency ambiguity
proposals.instruction: Headline uses acronyms for political bodies alongside generic terms like stars or deal without context.

proposals.name: Reader perspective prompts
proposals.instruction: Headline phrases the story as a direct question to the reader using could, do, or is this.

proposals.name: Ongoing investigation markers
proposals.instruction: Headline uses verbs indicating unfinished procedural reviews like under scrutiny or what happens next.

proposals.name: Curiosity Gap Question
proposals.instruction: Scores 1 if the headline is phrased as a direct question. Scores 0 if it is a declarative statement. Does not apply to rhetorical questions.
proposals.rationale: Questions explicitly provoke information-seeking, heavily driving user clicks.

proposals.name: First-Person Quotation
proposals.instruction: Scores 1 if a direct quote using first-person pronouns is included. Scores 0 for headlines with only indirect speech or no quotes.
proposals.rationale: Subjective voices increase emotional engagement and narrative pull for readers.

proposals.name: Superlative Or Absolute Framing
proposals.instruction: Scores 1 for extreme modifiers like "most", "longest", "all", or "world's". Scores 0 for standard comparative or neutral phrasing.
proposals.rationale: Readers are strongly attracted to record-breaking or maximally extreme phenomena.

proposals.name: Tech Or Digital Anomaly
proposals.instruction: Scores 1 for stories about hacked, malfunctioning, or bizarre digital technologies. Scores 0 for standard business tech news or non-digital topics.
proposals.rationale: Unusual tech failures blend modern relevance with morbid curiosity, driving high clicks.

proposals.name: Violation Of Deep Bodily Autonomy
proposals.instruction: Scores 1 for forced confinement, hacking, or medical forcing. Scores 0 for standard violence or accidental injury.
proposals.rationale: Readers click heavily on macabre or physically threatening individual scenarios.

proposals.name: Unsolved Or Ongoing Mystery
proposals.instruction: Scores 1 for words like "mystery" or signals of an unresolved search. Scores 0 for closed investigations or purely historical facts.
proposals.rationale: Ambiguity and the unknown compel users to click to find definitive answers.

proposals.name: Domestic Policy Without Named Elite
proposals.instruction: Scores 1 for major domestic rules lacking specific elite names. Scores 0 if specific politicians are named or impact is purely corporate.
proposals.rationale: Broad societal shifts drive high clicks even absent specific politicians.

proposals.name: Bureaucratic Or Institutional Inaction
proposals.instruction: Scores 1 for failure to open, suspensions, or quits. Scores 0 for proactive institutional bills, deals, or congratulatory actions.
proposals.rationale: Political friction and gridlock naturally generate high reader curiosity and click-through.

proposals.name: Implicit Deferral To Larger Context
proposals.instruction: Scores 1 when headline relies on undefined "new", "this", or "restrictions". Scores 0 if the core subject is explicitly named in text.
proposals.rationale: Readers click vague but urgent headlines to uncover the underlying missing context.

proposals.name: High-Emotion Celebrity Spectacle
proposals.instruction: Scores 1 for celebrity controversy, awards, or personal drama. Scores 0 for celebrity death, routine interviews, or business news.
proposals.rationale: Readers click soft-news cultural spectacles more than solemn or routine celebrity updates.

proposals.name: Factual Tragedy Without Singular Villain
proposals.instruction: Scores 1 for accidents or natural disasters. Scores 0 if death results from crime or explicit human targeting.
proposals.rationale: Intentional cruelty drives more reader outrage and urgency than accidental tragedies.

proposals.name: Unfamiliar Distant Geopolitics
proposals.instruction: Scores 1 for non-Western foreign politics lacking famous global figures. Scores 0 for domestic or major global power conflicts.
proposals.rationale: Average readers largely ignore complex foreign politics unless an elite hook exists.

proposals.name: Geographically Diffuse Crisis
proposals.instruction: Scores 1 if impact spans a large region without named local towns. Scores 0 if crisis is tied to a specific named city.
proposals.rationale: Diffuse regional impacts feel less immediate to readers than highly localized disasters.

proposals.name: Opaque Specialized Jargon
proposals.instruction: Scores 1 for specific program names without plain context. Scores 0 if the broad subject is clearly stated in the text.
proposals.rationale: Readers skip headlines requiring high prior knowledge, preferring immediately accessible text.

proposals.name: Distant Historical Speculation
proposals.instruction: Scores 1 for headlines about ancient or historical discoveries. Scores 0 for contemporary, ongoing, or recent past events.
proposals.rationale: Readers prioritize urgent present-day news over distant historical mysteries.

proposals.name: First-person quote excerpt
proposals.instruction: Headline opens with a quotation mark or uses first-person pronouns like I, my, or we.
proposals.upstream_parent: Editorial emphasis on human-interest victim or witness soundbites

proposals.name: Direct question format
proposals.instruction: Headline is formulated as a question (ending with a question mark or starting with interrogatives like why, could, will).
proposals.upstream_parent: Soft news beat or explanatory desk

proposals.name: Explicit fatality toll
proposals.instruction: Headline contains a specific number immediately followed by dead, dies, or kills.
proposals.upstream_parent: Breaking news wire style for mass-casualty events

proposals.name: UK political short-form
proposals.instruction: Headline relies on abbreviated UK political names or roles without first names (e.g., Labour MPs, UK PM, chancellor).

proposals.name: Tech or novelty app
proposals.instruction: Headline features a specific tech platform or digital gimmick (app, hack, YouTuber, dragon photo).

proposals.name: Premium paywalled term
proposals.instruction: Headline includes explicit lifestyle or cultural markers like therapist, luxury, or non-stop flight.

proposals.name: Dramatic quoted adjective
proposals.instruction: Headline relies entirely on an article followed by a dramatic adjective (e.g., 'sabotaged', 'offensive').
proposals.upstream_parent: Breaking news desk updating a developing story

proposals.name: Vague negative outcome verb
proposals.instruction: Headline uses indeterminate verbs like overshadow, quits, or fails rather than concrete actions.
proposals.upstream_parent: Political analysis or running story desk

proposals.name: Celebrity first-name-only
proposals.instruction: Headline refers to a celebrity or elite actor by first name or informal nickname (Adele, Selfie Kid).

proposals.name: High-burden institutional beat
proposals.instruction: Headline covers heavy institutional topics like taxes, migration policy, or border crossings without named individuals.
proposals.upstream_parent: Foreign policy or domestic affairs desk
